About: Photon Worldline & Vanishing Proper Time

Source

Lecture
17 — Photon
Simulation
Simulation 1 (guided inquiry): the photon worldline on a Minkowski diagram.
Concept
A photon travels along a lightlike worldline (45°) whose spacetime interval is exactly zero, so zero proper time elapses for the photon — a limit massive particles approach but never reach as v/c → 1.
Serves
Massless particle; proper time; representing photon worldlines in spacetime diagrams; explaining why proper time vanishes for photons.
Inquiry
Predict the photon's Δs² and Δτ between E₁ and E₂; predict what happens to a massive particle's proper time as you push v/c toward 1.
Misconception
"If I travel fast enough I can catch up with a photon and see it at rest" — addressed structurally (slider cannot reach v/c = 1, prediction option (d), and the friend persona prompt).

Reading the simulation

The massive particle ages by proper time Δτ along its worldline while the photon ages 0. Proper time is set by the worldline, not the mass.

Δτ = proper time along the worldline; E = γmc² = total relativistic energy, with γ = 1/√(1−(v/c)²), c = 1. Mass is in eV/c², so with c = 1 the energy E = γm comes out in eV. A photon is massless: Δτ = 0, and its energy E = hν is set by frequency, not mass.

When Show energies is on, the photon energy is E = hν (eV) at the chosen frequency (and wavelength λ = c/ν). The massive particle’s total energy is E = γmc² (eV). Push v/c → 1: Δτ → 0 while E → ∞, so a massive particle can never reach c; the photon is massless, so E = γmc² does not apply.

A pulse of light and a massive particle leave together — what does each clock record?

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

Guided Inquiry

1 · Two departures, one destination

Let’s set up the race. At E₁ a light pulse and a massive particle leave x = 0 together, both heading for x = 4 light-seconds. The pulse reaches that place at E₂; the particle, held below c, arrives later at E₂′. Along any worldline the spacetime interval is Δs² = −c²Δt² + Δx², and a carried clock records the proper time Δτ = √(−Δs²)/c.

2 · Predict — chasing the pulse

"If I travel fast enough I can catch up with a photon and see it at rest — just like running alongside a train."

Let’s put that to the test. The particle now runs at 99.5% of light speed. Measured from the particle, how fast do you think the pulse moves away?

3 · Predict — the pulse's interval

Now let’s measure the pulse’s own path. E₁ and E₂ are distinct events, four light-seconds apart in space and four seconds apart in time. Along the pulse’s worldline, what do you think Δs² comes to?

Have a look: Δτ for each worldline is now in the Readout panel.

4 · Predict — the photon's point of view

Here’s where it gets interesting. The particle’s Δτ shrinks as v/c rises, and along the pulse’s own worldline Δτ is zero. So what do you make of "the photon’s point of view"?

Watch the shaded wedge: that’s the Δτ gap. It narrows as v/c rises but never closes.

5 · A path of zero length

Let’s pull it all together. The 45° line is the edge of the light cone: events inside it are timelike-separated and their order is fixed, events outside are spacelike-separated, and events on it are null. A photon's worldline lies exactly on that edge, which is why it carries no proper time.

So no observer is ever carried along it: chasing light only tilts your own worldline nearer to 45°, never onto it.

The Physics

The photon worldline · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A light pulse and a massive particle leave the same event and head for the same place, four light-seconds away. The sim draws both worldlines on a spacetime diagram and reads out the proper time each one accumulates, which is how relativity measures the length of a path through spacetime.

What you'll learn

  • How the proper time along a worldline depends on the speed of whatever travels it.
  • What the spacetime interval Δs² is, and what its sign tells you about two events.
  • How energy is assigned to a massive particle and to a pulse of light.
  • What limits how close a massive worldline can lean toward the 45° line.
Both worldlines start at E₁ and reach x = 4 light-seconds. The pulse arrives at E₂, the particle later, at E₂′.

What's on screen

  • Pulse worldline (yellow): E₁ to E₂, with a glowing dot that moves along it. With Show energies on, it takes the pulse's wavelength colour.
  • Particle worldline (cyan): E₁ to E₂′ at the v/c you set. Its dot carries a τ label, the reading of a clock travelling with it.
  • Events E₁, E₂ and E₂′, a dashed line at ct = 4 where the pulse arrives, and a dashed vertical from E₂ to E₂′.
  • Axes: x across and ct up, both in light-seconds on equal scales.
  • Δτ wedge (violet): the shaded gap between the two worldlines, shown with Show comparison.
  • Readout panel: Δτ for each worldline, plus the energies when they are on.
See itSend both out from E₁ together at your current v/c. Watch for: the yellow dot reaching E₂ while the cyan dot is still climbing toward E₂′.

03

Proper time along a worldline

Between two events the sim uses the interval Δs² = −c²Δt² + Δx², with the time term negative. For the particle Δs² < 0, and a clock carried along its worldline reads the proper time Δτ = √(−Δs²)/c.

The interval, in the lecture sign convention.
The particle's Δt, Δs² and Δτ, with Δx = 4 light-seconds and c = 1.
v/c m

These sliders move the sim too.

  • Δt is the time on the frame's clocks. Δτ is the time on the clock the particle carries, always the smaller of the two.
  • Mass does not enter. Δτ depends on Δx and v/c only. Slide m and Δτ stays put.
  • Doubling v/c from 0.40 to 0.80 does not halve Δτ: it falls from 9.17 s to 3.00 s.
See itRun the finished worldline at m = 0.5, then at m = 4, with v/c unchanged. Watch for: the Δτ reading in the card staying the same while m changes.
04

The pulse's interval is zero

E₁ and E₂ are distinct events, four light-seconds apart in space and four seconds apart in time. Along the pulse Δx = cΔt, so the two terms of Δs² cancel exactly.

From the light signal to the proper time along it.
Three cases, set by the sign of Δs². The words are labels for those values.
The light cone at E₁. The 45° edge is where Δs² changes sign. The cyan line is the particle at v/c = 0.5.
  • Zero separation between two distinct events cannot happen in Euclidean geometry. The minus sign in Δs² allows it.
  • Every inertial observer measures light at c, so every one of them finds Δs² = 0 for this pair. The interval is invariant.
  • A massive particle's worldline stays inside the cone. Only a signal at c lies on its edge.
See itDraw both finished worldlines from E₁. Watch for: the yellow line at exactly 45° from E₁ to E₂, with the cyan line steeper than it.
05

No inertial frame travels with the pulse

The limit v/c → 1 for a massive particle. It is approached and never reached.
  • Δτ = Δx√(1−(v/c)²)/(v/c) is positive for every v/c < 1. At the slider's cap, 0.995, γ = 10.01 and Δτ = 0.40 s against Δt = 4.02 s.
  • Reaching c would need γ → ∞, which is infinite energy. That is why the slider stops short of 1.
  • The particle never closes in on the pulse. Velocities do not subtract the Newtonian way: for light, (c − v)/(1 − v/c) = c. Every inertial observer measures the pulse moving at c.
  • So Δτ = 0 along the pulse is not a stopped clock. It is a property of the worldline: no inertial frame moves at c, so no clock can be carried along it.

See itStep v/c through 0.50, 0.90, 0.99 and 0.995, with the wedge on. Watch for: the cyan line crowding the 45° line and the Δτ reading falling, without reaching zero.
06

Energy without mass

The massless limit. m = 0 does not make E or |p| zero. It ties them together.
  • The pulse has E = |p|c = hν, set by its frequency alone. At the default ν = 540 THz, λ = c/ν = 555 nm (green) and E = 2.23 eV. The ν slider covers 400–789 THz, 1.65–3.26 eV.
  • The particle has E = γmc², set by v/c and m. At v/c = 0.5 and m = 1 eV/c², E = 1.15 eV.
  • E = γmc² does not apply to the pulse. γ is undefined at v = c, and m = 0 would make the product 0 × ∞. The Readout's energy row uses E = hν for it.
  • Massless is not momentum-less: |p| = hν/c. The sim shows E only.
See itSwitch the energies on at your current settings. Watch for: the card listing E for the pulse and for the particle, and the pulse line drawn in its wavelength colour instead of plain yellow.
07

Where it matters

  • Cosmic-ray muons. A muon formed about 15 km up at v/c = 0.998 needs 50 µs by ground clocks to reach the surface. Its own clock reads 3.2 µs, against a rest-frame mean lifetime of 2.2 µs. This is the sim's Δτ = Δt/γ at work.
  • Sunlight. Light crosses 1 AU in 499 s (8.3 min) by Sun–Earth clocks. Its path has Δs² = 0, so there is no proper time to assign along it.
  • Solar sails. Light carries momentum |p| = E/c. Full absorption of sunlight at Earth's distance gives a pressure of about 4.5 µPa.
Go deeper: the pulse as a limit
  • Let m → 0 and v/c → 1 together, keeping E = γmc² fixed. Then |p|c/E = v/c → 1 and Δτ = Δx/((v/c)γ) → 0, which are the pulse's values.
  • This makes the pulse the limit of a family of massive worldlines. It does not give it a rest frame.
  • Along a null worldline τ cannot label the points, so the course uses an affine parameter λ instead.
08

Summary

In one line. Proper time is the length of a worldline, √(−Δs²)/c: positive and shrinking as v/c → 1 for the particle, zero for the pulse, and no inertial frame travels at c.

Key points

  • For the particle, Δτ = Δx√(1−(v/c)²)/(v/c), independent of its mass.
  • For the pulse Δx = cΔt, so Δs² = 0 in every inertial frame.
  • Δτ = 0 describes the pulse's worldline. It does not describe a viewpoint.
  • The pulse carries E = |p|c = hν, while the particle carries E = γmc².

Common mix-ups

  • "Run fast enough and you see the photon at rest." The pulse recedes at c from every inertial observer, and no massive body reaches c.
  • "The photon's clock is just stopped." A clock reading belongs to a frame, and none travels at c. Δτ = 0 is a fact about the path.
  • "Massless means no energy and no momentum." E = hν and |p| = hν/c. It is the rest mass that is zero.

Things to try on your own

  • Set v/c to 0.80 and note Δτ. Then jump to 0.99 and compare the two readings.
  • Turn the energies on, move ν across its range, and record the pulse's E at both ends.
  • With the energies on, set m = 5 and v/c = 0.995, then check the particle's E against γmc².
